title: Overview
text: Documentation Rapid Pi documentation Rapid Pi is the Pi coding agent compiled ahead of time to native code. It is the Pi you already use, with the same commands, sessions, settings, providers and extensions, as one executable. Against Pi as released on Node 24, it writes a large file through a tool call about 120 times faster, uses 8 times less CPU while a long answer streams, 7 times less over a session, and under a quarter of the memory. Install Rapid Pi One command on Linux, macOS, Windows and Android, or npm. Quickstart Run your first session, and use Rapid Pi next to Pi. Choose a build The default build, or the JIT build for heavy extensions. Extensions Run Pi extensions as they are, or compile them in. Benchmarks Time, CPU and memory against Pi on Bun and Node. Troubleshooting Check the compiled code, fix common problems, report a bug.

title: Overview
text: Pi is a TypeScript program. Stock Pi runs on Bun or Node, which parse its code at every launch and compile the hot parts with a just-in-time (JIT) compiler while it runs. Rapid Pi compiles every function of Pi to machine code when the executable is built, and stores Pi's modules already loaded. At launch there is nothing to parse and nothing to warm up. What stays the same: Your configuration. Rapid Pi reads ~/.pi/agent : your providers and logins, settings, sessions, skills, prompt templates and extensions. Pi's behavior. Rapid Pi is Pi's own source with a small set of fixes on top, not a rewrite. Each release is built on a named Pi release, and rapid-pi --version shows which. Your Pi installation. Rapid Pi installs next to Pi as rapid-pi . Both can stay installed. What changes is how Pi runs: it starts sooner, uses less CPU and memory over a session, and handles long answers and large file writes far more cheaply. See How it works and Benchmarks .

title: Overview
text: Platform Requirements Linux x86-64 or ARM64 with glibc 2.17 or later (Ubuntu 20.04+, Debian 11+, RHEL/Rocky 8+, Amazon Linux 2, Raspberry Pi OS 64-bit). musl is not supported. macOS macOS 13 or later on Apple silicon Windows Windows 10 (1809) or later, or Windows 11, on x64. Windows on ARM64 runs the x64 build in Windows 11's x64 emulation. Android Android 7 or later on 64-bit ARM, in Termux (see Android ) There is no build for Intel Macs.

title: Overview
text: This documentation covers what is specific to Rapid Pi: installing it, choosing a build, running extensions, performance and troubleshooting. For using the agent itself, Pi's documentation applies to Rapid Pi as written; replace pi with rapid-pi in its commands. To learn about Read in Pi's documentation Working in the terminal interface Use Pi in the terminal Connecting a provider and choosing a model Choose a model Resuming, branching and compacting sessions Sessions , Compaction Settings, context files, skills and prompt templates Configuration , Skills Writing extensions Extensions Scripting, JSON output, RPC and the SDK CLI , RPC , SDK An independent project Rapid Pi is an independent fork of Pi by OpenSec, not affiliated with Pi's authors or with Oven. It is built on Pi by Mario Zechner and contributors, and on Bun by Oven. Report Rapid Pi problems to Rapid Pi's issue tracker ; see Reporting a problem to tell which project a bug belongs to.

title: Installation
text: Get started Installation Install Rapid Pi with one command. The installer downloads the release for your system, checks its checksum and signature, and puts rapid-pi on your PATH. It does not change your Pi installation.

title: Installation
text: Linux on x86-64 or ARM64 with glibc 2.17 or later (Raspberry Pi 3 and later, AWS Graviton and Ampere included). musl distributions such as Alpine are not supported. macOS 13 or later on Apple silicon. There is no build for Intel Macs. Windows 10 (1809) or later, or Windows 11, on x64. Windows on ARM64 runs the x64 build, in Windows 11's x64 emulation. Android 7 or later on 64-bit ARM, in Termux. See Android (Termux) . Rapid Pi does not need Node.js, Bun or Pi. npm is only needed if you install with npm.

title: Installation
text: $ curl -fsSL https://rapid-pi.opensec.in/install.sh | sh $ curl -fsSL https://rapid-pi.opensec.in/install.sh | sh irm https://rapid-pi.opensec.in/install.ps1 | iex powershell -c "irm https://rapid-pi.opensec.in/install.ps1 | iex" On an older Windows 10 whose PowerShell only offers TLS 1.0, run these two lines in PowerShell instead: [Net.ServicePointManager]::SecurityProtocol = [Net.ServicePointManager]::SecurityProtocol -bor 3072 irm https://rapid-pi.opensec.in/install.ps1 | iex $ npm install -g --allow-scripts=rapid-pi rapid-pi --allow-scripts=rapid-pi lets npm run the package's install script, which puts the Windows executable in place. On macOS and Linux, the first run of rapid-pi downloads the release that matches the package's version. $ brew install opensec-git/tap/rapid-pi On macOS on Apple silicon and on Linux (x86-64 with AVX2, and ARM64). The formula installs the default build of the latest release, checked against its SHA256SUMS , and links rapid-pi into Homebrew's bin . For the JIT build or the x86-64 build for CPUs without AVX2, use the installer. scoop bucket add opensec-git https://github.com/opensec-git/scoop-bucket scoop install opensec-git/rapid-pi On Windows x64. The manifest in opensec-git/scoop-bucket installs the default build of the latest release, checked against the checksum in its SHA256SUMS , and puts rapid-pi on your PATH with a Scoop shim. For the JIT build, use the installer. [tools."github:ylstack1/RapidPi"] version = "latest" version_prefix = "bolt-v" asset_pattern = 'rapid-pi-{{ os(macos="darwin", windows="win32") }}-{{ arch() }}.tar.gz' platforms.windows-x64 = { asset_pattern = "rapid-pi-win32-x64.zip" } platforms.macos-arm64 = { rename_exe = { pi = "rapid-pi" }, filter_bins = "rapid-pi" } platforms.linux-x64 = { rename_exe = { pi = "rapid-pi" }, filter_bins = "rapid-pi" } platforms.linux-arm64 = { rename_exe = { pi = "rapid-pi" }, filter_bins = "rapid-pi" } $ mise install On macOS on Apple silicon, Linux (x86-64 with AVX2, and ARM64) and Windows x64, with mise's github backend. It installs the default build of the latest release, checked against the digest GitHub reports for it, renames the launcher pi to rapid-pi , and puts only rapid-pi on your PATH. For the JIT build, use the installer. The installer: Downloads the release for your platform and CPU, from the npm registry's CDN with GitHub as a fallback. Checks it against the release's SHA256SUMS , and checks the Ed25519 signature of SHA256SUMS against Rapid Pi's release key. A download that does not verify is not installed. (On macOS and Linux, the signature check needs OpenSSL 3 or an earlier Rapid Pi; without either, the installer checks the checksums only and says so.) Installs it to ~/.rapid-pi and links rapid-pi into ~/.local/bin . On Windows, it installs to %USERPROFILE%\.rapid-pi and asks before adding it to your PATH. It needs no administrator rights. Offers three optional extensions by OpenSec (subagents, a todo list and fast file search), and installs them only if you say yes. See OpenSec extensions . Then run rapid-pi in a project. Continue with the Quickstart .

title: Installation
text: In Termux from F-Droid or GitHub (the Google Play version has no glibc packages), run the same command as on Linux: $ curl -fsSL https://rapid-pi.opensec.in/install.sh | sh Rapid Pi is a glibc program and Android's libc is not glibc, so the installer first installs Termux's glibc ( pkg install glibc-repo && pkg install glibc , after asking), sets it as the executable's loader, and links rapid-pi into $PREFIX/bin . rapid-pi is a small launcher that starts Rapid Pi in Android's time zone and without Termux's LD_PRELOAD , which glibc cannot load; the programs Rapid Pi starts get it back. The installer also copies Termux's resolv.conf and hosts to $PREFIX/glibc/etc , where Termux's glibc reads them. rapid-pi: command not found ? ~/.local/bin is not on your PATH. Add export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" to your shell profile and open a new terminal.

title: Installation
text: Each platform has a default build and a JIT build. The installer picks the default build for your CPU. To choose another, set RAPIDPI_VARIANT . See Choose a build for when the JIT build is the better choice. Platform RAPIDPI_VARIANT Build Linux x86-64 x64 Default, for CPUs with AVX2 (Intel Haswell, AMD Zen and later) Linux x86-64 x64-baseline Any x86-64 CPU. Picked automatically when the CPU has no AVX2. Linux x86-64 x64-jit JIT on Linux ARM64, Termux arm64 Default, any 64-bit ARM CPU Linux ARM64, Termux arm64-jit JIT on macOS arm64 Default macOS arm64-jit JIT on, for heavy run-time extensions Windows x64 Default. Runs compiled code on CPUs with AVX2, and bytecode on others. Windows x64-jit JIT on $ curl -fsSL https://rapid-pi.opensec.in/install.sh | RAPIDPI_VARIANT=arm64-jit sh $ curl -fsSL https://rapid-pi.opensec.in/install.sh | RAPIDPI_VARIANT=x64-jit sh # x86-64 $ curl -fsSL https://rapid-pi.opensec.in/install.sh | RAPIDPI_VARIANT=arm64-jit sh # ARM64 and Termux $env:RAPIDPI_VARIANT = "x64-jit" powershell -c "irm https://rapid-pi.opensec.in/install.ps1 | iex" # ~/.zshrc or ~/.bashrc; use x64-jit on Linux x86-64 export RAPIDPI_VARIANT=arm64-jit On macOS and Linux, the npm package reads RAPIDPI_VARIANT every time it runs, so keep it set in your shell profile. If it is unset later, the next run switches back to the default build. On Windows, the npm package picks the build when it is installed or updated. Set the variable first, then install: $env:RAPIDPI_VARIANT = "x64-jit" npm install -g --allow-scripts=rapid-pi rapid-pi To change builds later, set or clear RAPIDPI_VARIANT and run the install again. rapid-pi update keeps the build you chose.

title: Installation
text: $ rapid-pi --version 1.4.0 (Rapid Pi 1.0.0, darwin-arm64, JIT off) The first number is the Pi release this build is made from. The rest is the Rapid Pi release, the platform, and whether the JIT is on. To check that Pi runs its compiled code, see Check the compiled code .

title: Installation
text: $ rapid-pi update # Rapid Pi only $ rapid-pi update --all # Rapid Pi and your extensions $ rapid-pi update --rollback # back to the build the last update replaced $ rapid-pi update --channel beta # take pre-releases too (stable: the latest release only) An update keeps the build it replaces; rapid-pi update --rollback puts it back without downloading anything, and running it again goes forward again. The channel is kept for the installation. With npm, run npm update -g rapid-pi ; the next run downloads the new release. With Homebrew, run brew upgrade rapid-pi ; rapid-pi update says so and changes nothing, and --rollback is not available. With Scoop, run scoop update rapid-pi , and scoop reset rapid-pi@<version> to go back to a version Scoop still keeps. With mise, run mise upgrade --bump github:ylstack1/RapidPi , and mise use -g github:ylstack1/RapidPi@<version> for another version. rapid-pi update and --rollback give these commands for a Rapid Pi that Scoop or mise installed, and change nothing. Running the installer again also updates.

title: Installation
text: Run the installer again and choose uninstall . It removes the Rapid Pi builds from ~/.rapid-pi , the one kept for a rollback among them, and the rapid-pi link. With npm, run npm uninstall -g rapid-pi , then delete ~/.rapid-pi/npm , where the npm package keeps the release it downloaded. With Homebrew, run brew uninstall rapid-pi ; with Scoop, scoop uninstall rapid-pi ; with mise, mise unuse -g github:ylstack1/RapidPi . Your Pi configuration in ~/.pi/agent belongs to Pi and is not removed.

title: Installation
text: Download a build from the latest release , check it against SHA256SUMS , unpack it, and run ./pi (on Windows, rapid-pi.exe ). Keep the unpacked folder together: the executable uses the files around it for themes, HTML export and image tools. Link to the executable rather than copying it. Download For rapid-pi-linux-x64.tar.xz Linux, CPUs with AVX2 rapid-pi-linux-x64-baseline.tar.xz Linux, any x86-64 CPU rapid-pi-linux-arm64.tar.xz Linux ARM64, any 64-bit ARM CPU (in Termux, use the installer) rapid-pi-darwin-arm64.tar.xz macOS on Apple silicon rapid-pi-win32-x64.zip Windows x64 The JIT builds are rapid-pi-linux-x64-jit.tar.xz , rapid-pi-linux-arm64-jit.tar.xz , rapid-pi-darwin-arm64-jit.tar.xz and rapid-pi-win32-x64-jit.zip . To check a download: $ sha256sum -c --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS macOS: downloaded with a browser A browser marks downloads as quarantined, and macOS then refuses Rapid Pi's ad-hoc signed executable ( zsh: killed , or "cannot verify the developer"). Install with the installer or npm, which do not quarantine, or remove the attribute from the unpacked folder: xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine rapid-pi-darwin-arm64 .

title: Installation
text: Set these in the environment of the installer: curl ... | NAME=value sh on macOS and Linux, $env:NAME = "value" before the command on Windows. Variable Effect RAPIDPI_VARIANT The build to install (see Builds ). RAPIDPI_VERSION A release tag such as bolt-v1.0.0 . Default: the latest release. RAPIDPI_CHANNEL stable (the latest release; the default) or beta (the newest release, pre-releases included), for this installation and its updates. RAPIDPI_INSTALL Where to install. Default: ~/.rapid-pi (Windows: %USERPROFILE%\.rapid-pi ). RAPIDPI_BIN_DIR macOS and Linux: where to link rapid-pi . Default: ~/.local/bin . RAPIDPI_NO_PATH=1 Windows: do not add Rapid Pi to your PATH. RAPIDPI_YES=1 Do not ask: take the default action, install no extensions, and do not offer to start Rapid Pi. RAPIDPI_EXTENSIONS yes or no : whether to install OpenSec's optional extensions without asking. RAPIDPI_SOURCE Where to download the executable from: auto (npm, then GitHub; the default), npm or github . Checksums and signatures always come from the GitHub release. RAPIDPI_NPM_REGISTRY An npm registry or mirror. Default: https://registry.npmjs.org . RAPIDPI_CONNECTIONS macOS and Linux: connections to download over at once. Default: 4.

title: Quickstart
text: Get started Quickstart If you use Pi already, Rapid Pi works with what you have: run rapid-pi instead of pi . If you are new to Pi, this page takes you from install to a first finished task. Install Rapid Pi $ curl -fsSL https://rapid-pi.opensec.in/install.sh | sh On Windows or with npm, see Installation . Start it in a project $ cd my-project $ rapid-pi Rapid Pi opens Pi's terminal interface in the current folder. That folder is what the agent reads and edits. Connect a model If you have used Pi, your providers and logins are already there. Otherwise type /login and pick a provider, or set a provider's API key in your environment (for example ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or OPENAI_API_KEY ) before starting. Switch models with /model . See Pi's Choose a model . Give it a task Type what you want done and press Enter, for example Find where the config file is parsed and add a test for an empty file. The agent reads files, runs commands and edits code, and shows each step as it goes. Press Escape to stop it.

title: Quickstart
text: $ rapid-pi "Explain the build setup" # start with a prompt $ rapid-pi -p "List the TODOs in src/" # run one prompt, print the answer, exit $ rapid-pi -c # continue the last session here $ rapid-pi -r # pick a session to resume $ rapid-pi --model sonnet:high # a model, with a thinking level $ rapid-pi @README.md "Summarize this" # include a file rapid-pi --help lists every option. They are Pi's options; Pi's CLI reference describes them in full.

title: Quickstart
section: Using Rapid Pi next to Pi
text: Rapid Pi and Pi share ~/.pi/agent , so both see the same: providers, logins and API keys ( auth.json , models.json ); settings ( settings.json ); sessions, which either can resume; extensions, skills, prompt templates and themes. Install an extension with either command and both load it: $ rapid-pi install npm:opensec-pi-todo A tool that starts Pi by running pi keeps using stock Pi. To make it use Rapid Pi, point it at rapid-pi : see Integrations .

title: Quickstart
text: Choose a build When to use the JIT build instead of the default. Extensions How extensions run in Rapid Pi, and which need the JIT build. Use Pi in the terminal Pi's guide to the interface, commands and shortcuts. Sessions Resume, branch and export your work, in Pi's docs.

title: Choose a build
text: Guides Choose a build Every platform has two builds. Pi itself is compiled ahead of time in both. They differ in what happens to code that is loaded while Pi runs, such as extensions.

title: Choose a build
text: Default (JIT off) JIT build (JIT on) Pi's own code Compiled machine code Compiled machine code Extensions loaded at run time Interpreted Interpreted, then JIT-compiled as they warm up bun:ffi , heavy eval / new Function bun:ffi does not work Works Memory Lowest Higher once the JIT has compiled something rapid-pi --version ends in JIT off JIT on A JIT (just-in-time compiler) turns code into machine code while the program runs. Rapid Pi's default build has none: Pi was compiled before you ran it, so it does not need one, and it saves the JIT's compiler threads, warm-up and memory.

title: Choose a build
text: No extensions, or light ones (a todo list, UI panels, small hooks, most extensions): the default build. These spend their time waiting on the model, files or processes, so how their code runs does not show. Extensions that do heavy work in JavaScript (search, parsing, analysis over many files): the JIT build. On the default build their code is interpreted. Extensions that use bun:ffi , such as pi-fff: the JIT build. On the default build they fail with bun:ffi requires the JIT , because native calls through bun:ffi are generated by the JIT. Extensions you use every day and can build yourself : compile them into the default build, where they run as machine code. See Compile extensions in . If you are unsure, the JIT build is the safe choice: it costs within about 5% of the default build in CPU and memory.

title: Choose a build
text: The same Pi session on both builds, Rapid Pi 0.7.3, against Pi 1.1.0 on stock Bun. Lower is better. Benchmark Default JIT build Pi on Bun Linux: CPU, interactive session (5 prompts) 309 ms 324 ms 913 ms Linux: ready to type 47 ms 52 ms 143 ms macOS: CPU, interactive session (5 prompts) 175 ms 175 ms 555 ms macOS: memory, interactive session 100 MB 104 MB 208 MB And what it changes for an extension. An example extension command scans a 16.8 MB file character by character (Linux, Rapid Pi 0.7.3): How the extension runs Launch to ready The command Compiled in, default build 52 ms 55 ms Loaded at run time, default build 91 ms 1,315 ms Loaded at run time, JIT build 83 ms 48 ms Loaded at run time, Pi on Bun 244 ms 45 ms Most real extensions are not like this command. Measured on Windows with nine popular extensions from npm, run-time extensions on the default build started fastest, used the least memory, and took the same time for their usual actions as with the JIT on. The exception was an extension doing heavy JavaScript work itself: one report took 838 ms with the JIT off and 154 ms with it on.

title: Choose a build
text: $ curl -fsSL https://rapid-pi.opensec.in/install.sh | RAPIDPI_VARIANT=arm64-jit sh Back to the default: RAPIDPI_VARIANT=arm64 . $ curl -fsSL https://rapid-pi.opensec.in/install.sh | RAPIDPI_VARIANT=x64-jit sh Back to the default: RAPIDPI_VARIANT=x64 (or x64-baseline on a CPU without AVX2). $env:RAPIDPI_VARIANT = "x64-jit" powershell -c "irm https://rapid-pi.opensec.in/install.ps1 | iex" Back to the default: $env:RAPIDPI_VARIANT = "x64" . export RAPIDPI_VARIANT=arm64-jit # x64-jit on Linux On macOS and Linux, the npm package reads RAPIDPI_VARIANT on every run and downloads that build on first use. Remove it to go back to the default. On Windows, the npm package picks the build when it is installed or updated: set $env:RAPIDPI_VARIANT = "x64-jit" , then run npm install -g --allow-scripts=rapid-pi rapid-pi again. Clear the variable and install again to go back. Then check with rapid-pi --version . rapid-pi update keeps the build you chose.

title: Extensions
text: Guides Extensions Pi extensions and Pi packages work in Rapid Pi without changes. They are found, installed and configured exactly as in Pi. What differs is how their code runs, which depends on the build.

title: Extensions
text: Rapid Pi loads extensions from the same places as Pi: ~/.pi/agent/extensions , a project's .pi/extensions , Pi packages, and -e <path> on the command line. $ rapid-pi install --rapid-pi npm:opensec-pi-todo # install for Rapid Pi only $ rapid-pi list # list installed packages $ rapid-pi update --extensions # update them $ rapid-pi remove --rapid-pi npm:opensec-pi-todo # remove one $ rapid-pi config # turn resources on and off rapid-pi install and rapid-pi remove change the shared packages list used by both Pi and Rapid Pi. Add --rapid-pi to change only Rapid Pi's package overrides, which inherit the shared list and can add, exclude or replace packages (see Configuration ). Rapid Pi installs packages with its own package manager when npm is not installed. A run-time extension's own dependencies resolve as they do on Node, through its package.json . Writing extensions is covered by Pi's Extensions guide.

title: Extensions
text: Loaded at run time, default build Loaded at run time, JIT build Compiled in Changes needed None None Usually none (see the checklist ) Startup cost TypeScript compiled at each start TypeScript compiled at each start None Hot code runs as Bytecode interpreter Interpreter, then JIT Machine code Update the extension Edit and restart Edit and restart Rebuild the executable (about 10 s) Best for Light extensions, trying things out Many or heavy third-party extensions Extensions you use every day For most extensions the interpreter makes no visible difference: they spend their time waiting on the model, files or processes. It matters for extensions that do heavy work in JavaScript. See Choose a build for measurements.

title: Extensions
section: Extensions that need the JIT build
text: Extensions that call native libraries through bun:ffi fail on the default build with bun:ffi requires the JIT . An example is pi-fff , which replaces Pi's find and grep with FFF, a fast, pre-indexed file search in Rust. Extensions that run a lot of code they generate with eval , new Function or vm : that code is only ever interpreted on the default build. Extensions that do heavy work in JavaScript : they work on the default build, more slowly. Install the JIT build with RAPIDPI_VARIANT , as described in Switch builds .

title: Extensions
text: Some extensions start more Pi processes, for example to run subagents. If such an extension runs the pi command, its subagents run on stock Pi (or fail when Pi is not installed). Check the extension's settings for the command it runs. For pi-subagents , set: export PI_SUBAGENT_PI_BINARY=rapid-pi

title: Extensions
text: The installer offers three extensions that OpenSec maintains for Rapid Pi. They are prebuilt for Rapid Pi's runtime, so they load without being transpiled. The installer uses --rapid-pi to keep them out of Pi's shared list, as Pi on Node cannot run them. It installs the versions each release pins. Package What it does opensec-pi-subagents Specialized agents in separate sessions that inherit the parent's model and thinking level, with parallel workflows and scheduled jobs. opensec-pi-todo A todo list for the model, shown as a live panel above the editor. It survives /reload and compaction. opensec-pi-fff Fast file and content search: find, grep and @-mentions, as fast on the default build as with the JIT. Not offered when @ff-labs/pi-fff is installed. $ rapid-pi install --rapid-pi npm:opensec-pi-subagents $ rapid-pi install --rapid-pi npm:opensec-pi-todo $ rapid-pi install --rapid-pi npm:opensec-pi-fff

title: Extensions
text: An extension compiled into the executable runs as machine code like Pi itself, with no startup cost. On Linux and macOS, rapid-pi compile compiles the extensions you have installed into your Rapid Pi: $ rapid-pi compile # the extensions installed here $ rapid-pi compile --exclude big-bundle # all but these (--only: just these) $ rapid-pi compile --off # the release's executable again It downloads its release's runtime and compile kit, checks them against the release's signature, and builds in about 20 seconds. The build it replaces is kept ( rapid-pi update --rollback puts it back), and rapid-pi update compiles the same extensions into each new release. An extension compiled in is used while its installed copy is unchanged; one changed since is loaded from its files, with a warning to compile it in again. To build with a manifest of your own (on Windows too), use a Rapid Pi build environment (see Building ): Write a manifest A module whose default export lists the extensions' factories: import type { InlineExtension } from "@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent"; import gitGuard from "./extensions/git-guard.ts"; import wordCount from "./extensions/word-count.ts"; const plugins: InlineExtension[] = [ { name: "git-guard", factory: gitGuard }, { name: "word-count", factory: wordCount }, ]; export default plugins; Everything in the manifest's folder is built with it, including its node_modules (run npm install there first). Build $ scripts/build-pi.sh --plugins my-plugins/plugins.ts --out out/rapid-pi-plugins On Windows: scripts\build-pi.ps1 -Plugins my-plugins\plugins.ts -Out out\rapid-pi-plugins . Check $ BUN_STATIC_HEAP_VERBOSE=1 out/rapid-pi-plugins/pi --version 2>&1 | grep "image registered" [aot] image registered: true A named extension is a built-in, builtin:<name> : -builtin:<name> in the extensions setting turns it off. If the same extension is also installed at run time, the run-time copy takes over and the compiled-in one steps aside. The full guide, with workers, embedded files and training a profile, is Porting Pi plugins to Rapid Pi .

title: Extensions
text: These are the rules for any code bundled into one executable. Most extensions already follow them. Import Pi from its packages ( @earendil-works/pi-coding-agent , @earendil-works/pi-ai , @earendil-works/pi-tui , typebox ) and list them as peerDependencies , so that no second copy is bundled. Use static imports. An import of a path computed at run time cannot be bundled. Use a table of literal imports instead. Import files instead of reading them next to the source : import prompt from "./prompt.md" with { type: "text" } . Keep the factory light. Start processes, sockets and timers from session_start or the command that needs them. Do not replace the standard objects' methods. Rapid Pi freezes them, so Array.prototype.map = ... throws. Polyfills that only add what is missing are fine.

title: Extensions
text: Extensions run inside the Pi process with your permissions, whether they are loaded at run time or compiled in. Only install extensions from sources you trust.

title: Integrations
text: Guides Integrations Anything that runs Pi can run Rapid Pi: it takes the same arguments, speaks the same JSON and RPC protocols, and reads the same configuration. Point the tool at rapid-pi instead of pi .

title: Integrations
text: Agent managers, editors and web interfaces start Pi by running a command, usually pi . Most let you set that command. Set it to rapid-pi , or to the full path that command -v rapid-pi prints. A tool that bundles its own copy of Pi, locked to a version, runs that copy and not Rapid Pi, unless it lets you choose the Pi executable.

title: Integrations
text: Paseo runs Pi through its pi provider. To run every Pi agent on Rapid Pi, change that provider's command in ~/.paseo/config.json : { "agents": { "providers": { "pi": { "command": ["rapid-pi"] } } } } Or add Rapid Pi as a provider of its own, next to Pi. "extends": "pi" tells Paseo to drive it the way it drives Pi; command only changes the executable: { "agents": { "providers": { "rapid-pi": { "extends": "pi", "label": "Rapid Pi", "command": ["rapid-pi"] } } } } Restart Paseo, then pick Rapid Pi in the app or run paseo run --provider rapid-pi "your task" .

title: Integrations
text: Pi's non-interactive modes work as documented by Pi: $ rapid-pi -p "Summarize the open TODOs" # print mode: answer, then exit $ rapid-pi -p --mode json "Run the tests" # a stream of JSON events $ rapid-pi --mode rpc # controlled by another program over stdio See Pi's CLI , JSON and RPC references. A one-shot rapid-pi -p starts and finishes several times faster than Pi on Bun or Node, which adds up in scripts and CI. Pi's TypeScript SDK embeds Pi in your own program; that program runs on its own runtime, not on Rapid Pi.

title: Integrations
text: Rapid Pi runs in tmux, zmx and other multiplexers as Pi does. It also writes less to the terminal: on Linux a session in tmux takes about 28 MB of Rapid Pi's own memory, against 87 MB for Pi on Bun. See Pi's Run Pi in tmux for tmux settings. If a terminal draws the screen wrongly while the interface scrolls, start Rapid Pi with PI_TUI_SCROLL_ROWS=0 , which redraws changed rows instead of scrolling them. tmux, zmx, xterm, kitty, Ghostty and VTE terminals do not need it.

title: Integrations
text: Rapid Pi needs nothing from a Linux image but glibc 2.17 or later. The installer also needs curl or wget , and tar . Install it in the image with RAPIDPI_YES=1 , which takes the defaults without asking: RUN curl -fsSL https://rapid-pi.opensec.in/install.sh | RAPIDPI_YES=1 sh ENV PATH="/root/.local/bin:$PATH" Memory limits. Count the executable too: its code is file-backed memory that the kernel charges to the container. Rapid Pi runs with a limit of about 100 MB, at twice the CPU and with pauses; 256 MB or more leaves it alone. CPU limits. With --cpus , Rapid Pi starts fewer threads. Address-space limits. The compiled code needs about 10 GB of virtual address space. It is reserved, not used. Under a tighter ulimit -v , Rapid Pi runs from bytecode, more slowly; see Notices at startup . Pi's Isolate Pi covers running the agent in a container safely.

title: Configuration
text: Guides Configuration Rapid Pi has no configuration of its own: it reads Pi's. A few environment variables control the Rapid Pi executable itself, for diagnostics and tuning.

title: Configuration
text: Rapid Pi and Pi share the agent directory, ~/.pi/agent , and a project's .pi folder: File or folder Holds settings.json Settings: default model, theme, extensions on and off, and more auth.json , models.json Logins and API keys; custom providers and models sessions/ Saved sessions extensions/ , prompts/ Your extensions and prompt templates mcp.json MCP servers Pi's Configuration , Settings and Environment variables pages apply to Rapid Pi as written. PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR moves the agent directory, and PI_OFFLINE=1 (or --offline ) turns off network operations at startup.

title: Configuration
section: Shared packages and Rapid Pi overrides
text: rapid-pi install and rapid-pi remove update the shared packages list, just as Pi does. They do not create a separate copy. They also drop Rapid Pi's own entry for that package in the same settings file (a replacement, an addition or an exclusion), so Rapid Pi then loads what the shared list declares: remove stops both from loading the package, and install npm:tools@2 is not hidden by a Rapid Pi entry for npm:tools@1 . Use --rapid-pi to change only rapidPi.packages , which Pi ignores. These examples use fictional package names: $ rapid-pi install --rapid-pi npm:@example/bolt-tools $ rapid-pi remove --rapid-pi npm:@example/shared-tools rapidPi.packages extends packages in the same settings file. Entries are applied in order: a package adds to the inherited list or replaces an entry with the same identity; a -source string excludes it. For example: { "packages": ["npm:@example/shared-tools", "npm:@example/theme"], "rapidPi": { "packages": ["-npm:@example/shared-tools", "npm:@example/bolt-tools"] } } Rapid Pi loads @example/theme and @example/bolt-tools ; Pi still loads @example/shared-tools and @example/theme . Later changes to the shared list remain inherited. Package objects with resource filters work in either list. Identity matching uses the npm package name, the Git repository, or the resolved local path, ignoring versions and Git refs. remove --rapid-pi removes an explicit override and, if the package is inherited, records an exclusion. install --rapid-pi replaces a matching exclusion with the package. Add --local to either command to edit .pi/settings.json instead of global settings. Each file's overrides affect only its own shared list; project/global precedence is unchanged. A project exclusion does not exclude a global package. These are configuration overrides, not separate installations. Pi and Rapid Pi share installed package files, so selecting different versions or Git refs of the same package can replace the files used by both. Existing configurations: before 0.9.1, rapidPi.packages was an independent list, copied from packages on the first rapid-pi install or removal. Rapid Pi converts such a copy once, at its next start: each shared package missing from the copy gets a -source exclusion, entries identical to their shared entry are dropped (so future shared changes apply to them), and entries that differ or exist only for Rapid Pi are kept. Rapid Pi then loads what it loaded before, and packages added to packages later are inherited. Rapid Pi marks the list with "packagesOverlay": true whenever it writes it; an unmarked list without -source entries is taken for an old copy, so add the mark to a list you write by hand. The installer uses --rapid-pi for OpenSec's optional Bun-only extensions. The existing startup repair for older installations still moves those extensions out of the shared list, but does not copy other shared packages.

title: Configuration
text: These are read by the Rapid Pi executable at run time. Variable Effect RAPIDPI_VARIANT The build the installer or the npm package installs. See Choose a build . RAPIDPI_HOME npm package: where downloaded builds are kept. Default: ~/.rapid-pi . BUN_AOT=0 Ignore the compiled code and run Pi from bytecode. Use it to tell whether a problem comes from the compiled code. BUN_STATIC_HEAP_VERBOSE=1 Report how the compiled code and prebuilt heap were loaded. PI_TIMING=1 Pi's startup timings, including each extension's factory. PI_TUI_SCROLL_ROWS=0 Redraw every changed row instead of scrolling rows that only moved, for a terminal that does not scroll a region correctly. BUN_CONFIG_HTTP_KEEPALIVE_TIMEOUT=N Seconds an idle connection to a server waits to be reused when the server does not say. Default: 4, as in Node. BUN_JSC_numberOfGCMarkers=N Threads that mark during a garbage collection. Default: 2. MIMALLOC_PURGE_HOLES_MIN_INTERVAL=N Milliseconds between returns of freed memory to the system. Default: 250. Lower returns memory sooner, for more CPU. JITI_FS_CACHE=false Do not keep the transpiled source of run-time extensions (kept in cache/jiti of the agent directory). The installer has its own variables; see Installer options .

title: Configuration
text: Rapid Pi does not read a .env file from the working directory. Pi on Bun does, because Bun loads one into every program's environment; Pi on Node does not. A project's .env (its API keys, its proxy settings) belongs to the project. Set what Pi should see in the shell that starts it.

title: Benchmarks
text: Reference Benchmarks Rapid Pi 1.0.0 against Pi 1.4.0 as released, run by stock Bun 1.4.4, Node 22 and Node 24, on GitHub's Linux x86-64, Linux ARM64 and Windows runners and an Apple M5 Mac. Lower is better in every row.

title: Benchmarks
text: The same work for every build. Each build runs the same prompts against a local server that replays the same model responses, so there is no network or provider variance. Pi as released. "Pi on Bun" and "Pi on Node" are Pi 1.4.0 from its npm package ( @earendil-works/pi-coding-agent ), not Rapid Pi's tree. Rapid Pi is the release's code built on its runtimes. Every downloaded build is checked against its checksums. Interleaved. Builds take turns, so a change in the machine's state affects all of them alike. Times to start and sessions are medians of 21 runs. CPU time is user plus system time of the process. Memory is the process's resident memory (on Windows, the working set). The benchmark scripts, the method in full and the raw data are in the repository: BENCHMARKS.md and bench/results .

title: Benchmarks
section: Why a large file write takes so long on stock Pi
text: Those two to three minutes are not the disk. A model writes a file by streaming the write tool call's arguments, the whole file, a few characters at a time, so a 400 KB file arrives in thousands of chunks. For every chunk, stock Pi parses the whole tool call again, redraws the screen even when nothing shown has changed, and highlights every line of the file. Each chunk costs more than the last, and the total grows with the square of the file's size. Rapid Pi parses again only once the arguments have grown by an eighth, draws a frame only when what is shown changes, and highlights only the lines it shows. In the benchmark the model streams as fast as it can, so the cost shows as wall time. With a real model, which streams more slowly, it shows as CPU.

title: Benchmarks
section: Why streaming and long sessions cost less
text: Streaming. Stock Pi redraws the message every time a few words arrive, and each redraw re-lexes the whole Markdown, re-wraps every block and re-highlights every code block. Rapid Pi keeps what it has rendered and redoes only the last block or two, with highlighted code cached. The screen shows the same output, line for line. Long sessions. Every request sends the whole conversation to the model again, and stock Pi serializes all of it from scratch each time, so each prompt costs more than the last. Rapid Pi builds each request from the previous one's bytes plus what is new. The bytes sent are identical. Measurements, not guarantees Each table comes from one machine. On other hardware the times differ; what carries over is the comparison.

title: How it works
text: Reference How it works Rapid Pi does at build time the work that Bun or Node does at every launch: parsing Pi's code, loading its modules and compiling its hot functions. What is left at launch is mapping the result from the executable and running Pi.

title: How it works
text: Stock Pi is JavaScript run by Bun or Node. Every launch, the runtime reads Pi's code, parses it into bytecode, loads and runs every module, and starts Pi in an interpreter. As Pi runs, a JIT compiler watches which functions are hot and what types flow through them, and compiles those to machine code. Until then they are interpreted, and the JIT itself costs CPU, threads and memory.

title: How it works
text: Bundle and compile to bytecode Bun bundles Pi's modules into one program and compiles every function to JavaScriptCore bytecode. Load Pi into a heap Pi's modules are loaded and evaluated, and the resulting heap is saved: the prebuilt heap. It holds Pi's functions, classes and data already set up. Compile every function ahead of time An ahead-of-time compiler turns every function into optimized x86-64 or ARM64 machine code, through B3, the back end of JavaScriptCore's top-tier JIT. Without a running program to watch, it works from what it can prove about the code: whole program type inference, inlining of small functions and array callbacks, fast copies of hot loops, and guarded fast paths with a generic path for the unusual case. Lay it out for startup A training profile, recorded from scripted Pi sessions, orders the code and the heap so that a launch touches as few pages as possible. Regular expressions that Pi builds at run time are compiled ahead of time too. Write one executable The Bun runtime, Pi's bundled program, the prebuilt heap and the machine code go into a single executable.

title: How it works
text: The executable checks that its compiled code fits the engine and the CPU, maps the prebuilt heap and the code from its own file, and runs Pi's main() . Nothing is parsed and nothing is compiled. Pi's modules run their top-level code, as compiled code. If a check fails (an older CPU, a tight address-space limit), the executable says so in one line and runs Pi from bytecode instead: correct, but slower. See Notices at startup .

title: How it works
text: The code and the prebuilt heap are file-backed. Pages that are only read are shared with the system's file cache, and the system can drop them under memory pressure. A process's own memory is what it writes. No JIT in the default build: no compiler threads, no JIT code caches, no profiling data. No bytecode is kept for functions that have machine code.

title: How it works
section: Why it uses less CPU over a session
text: Compiled code accounts for the faster start. Over a session, most of the difference comes from Pi itself: Rapid Pi carries fixes to Pi's TypeScript where Pi redid work over the whole conversation or the whole streamed output at every step. Examples: a streamed tool call is parsed once, not again for every chunk; a long answer is redrawn incrementally; a command's output is written as it arrives. These fixes are in Rapid Pi's source, on top of Pi's.

title: How it works
text: Code loaded at run time is not compiled ahead of time. On the default build it is interpreted. Use the JIT build or compile extensions in . No type feedback. A warmed-up JIT specializes on the types it sees; the ahead-of-time compiler uses what it can prove. Code with predictable types gets the fast paths. One executable per Pi release. Each build is made from one Pi release and one engine.

title: How it works
text: The ahead-of-time compiler builds on Jarred Sumner's work for Bun, oven-sh/WebKit#743 . Rapid Pi ports it to x86-64, macOS on ARM64 and Windows, and adds its own code generation and runtime work. Pi's source with Rapid Pi's changes is in packages/ of the repository; the engine changes are in patches/ . The full design is in ARCHITECTURE.md .

title: Security
text: Reference Security Every Rapid Pi release is signed. The installers verify what they download before installing it, need no administrator rights, and change nothing outside your own folders.

title: Security
text: Each release publishes SHA256SUMS , the SHA-256 checksum of every file, and SHA256SUMS.sig , an Ed25519 signature of that file made with Rapid Pi's release key. The public key is in the repository as keys/release.pub and inside the installers: -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY----- MCowBQYDK2VwAyEAoLboJqtKaoISPqffk03vHZr+1sRBG3uIRIWeKOew+aY= -----END PUBLIC KEY----- The installers and rapid-pi update refuse a download whose checksum or signature does not verify. Checksums and signatures always come from the GitHub release, so a download from the npm registry's CDN is checked against them too.

title: Security
text: $ sha256sum -c --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS $ openssl pkeyutl -verify -pubin -inkey release.pub -rawin -in SHA256SUMS -sigfile SHA256SUMS.sig The second command needs OpenSSL 3 or later; macOS's own openssl (LibreSSL) cannot check Ed25519, but Homebrew's openssl@3 can.

title: Security
text: Installs into your home folder ( ~/.rapid-pi , or %USERPROFILE%\.rapid-pi on Windows) and links one command. It needs no administrator rights and changes no security setting. On Windows, asks before adding Rapid Pi to your PATH. Installs OpenSec's optional extensions only when you say yes, at the versions the release pins, and only if the registry's package matches the pinned integrity hash. Does not touch your Pi installation. In ~/.pi/agent it only installs the extensions you accepted.

title: Security
text: Rapid Pi runs Pi's tools with your permissions, as Pi does: the agent can read and write files and run commands in your project. Pi's Run Pi safely and Isolate Pi apply to Rapid Pi. Extensions run inside the Pi process with your permissions. Only install extensions from sources you trust. A project's .env is not loaded into Rapid Pi's environment. See .env files . Crash reports contain an encoded stack trace and nothing else: no file names, paths or data of yours. See A crash .

title: Security
text: Report security issues privately through GitHub's private vulnerability reporting , not in public issues. We acknowledge the report, investigate, and coordinate a fix and disclosure with you. In scope: the Rapid Pi runtime and engine changes, the release executables, and the scripts and installers in the repository. Vulnerabilities in Pi itself belong to Pi ; vulnerabilities in Bun or JavaScriptCore that Rapid Pi does not change belong to their projects.

title: Troubleshooting
text: Help Troubleshooting Most problems are a PATH, a platform requirement or an extension. Start by checking that Rapid Pi runs its compiled code, then find your symptom below.

title: Troubleshooting
text: $ BUN_STATIC_HEAP_VERBOSE=1 rapid-pi --version [aot] image of 42467328 bytes mapped, 35635200 of them code [static heap] 94109736 bytes in executable, mapped: true [aot] image registered: true 1.4.0 (Rapid Pi 1.0.0, linux-x64, JIT off) image registered: true means Pi runs its ahead-of-time compiled code. Without the variable, a healthy executable prints nothing extra.

title: Troubleshooting
text: When the compiled code cannot be used, Rapid Pi prints one line and runs Pi from bytecode. Pi works correctly, but starts more slowly and uses more CPU. rapid-pi: the executable's ahead-of-time compiled code is not used (<reason>); running from bytecode Reason Cause and fix the address space for it is not available An address-space limit ( ulimit -v , RLIMIT_AS , or vm.overcommit_memory=2 ). The compiled code needs about 10 GB of virtual address space, reserved, not used. Raise or remove the limit. this CPU lacks an instruction set the code was compiled for The Linux x64 build on a CPU without AVX2. Install the x64-baseline build ( RAPIDPI_VARIANT=x64-baseline ). the image is not one for this engine , the image could not be mapped executable , the prebuilt heap could not be mapped A damaged executable, or a system that forbids executable file mappings. Reinstall and check SHA256SUMS . Report it if it persists. the executable could not be loaded where its prebuilt heap expects it macOS only. Report it, with sw_vers and how Rapid Pi was started. One failure is fatal instead: the executable's ahead-of-time code image was rejected by the engine . It should not happen with a release build. Run with BUN_AOT=0 and report it.

title: Troubleshooting
text: ~/.local/bin is not on your PATH. Add export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" to your shell profile. On Windows, open a new terminal after installing, or run the installer again and let it add Rapid Pi to your PATH.

title: Troubleshooting
section: GLIBC_2.xx not found , or No such file or directory on Linux
text: The system uses musl (Alpine) or a glibc older than 2.17. Rapid Pi needs glibc 2.17 or later.

title: Troubleshooting
text: The CPU has no SSE4.2 (older than Intel Nehalem, 2008, or AMD Bulldozer, 2011). No Rapid Pi build runs on it.

title: Troubleshooting
text: An extension calls into a native library through bun:ffi , which works only on the JIT build. The message names the extension and gives the command that installs the JIT build ( Switch builds ); rapid-pi doctor lists every extension that uses bun:ffi .

title: Troubleshooting
text: On the default build, extensions loaded at run time are interpreted. Use the JIT build , or compile the extension in .

title: Troubleshooting
section: Subagents run stock Pi, or fail to start
text: The extension starts subagents with the pi command. Point it at rapid-pi : see Extensions that start Pi .

title: Troubleshooting
section: A theme, HTML export or image tools are missing
text: The executable was moved away from the files around it. Keep the installed folder together, and link to the executable instead of copying it.

title: Troubleshooting
text: Check that the compiled code is used (above). Run with PI_TIMING=1 to see slow extension factories. The first start after a reboot or an install also reads the executable from disk.

title: Troubleshooting
section: The screen draws wrongly while scrolling
text: Start Rapid Pi with PI_TUI_SCROLL_ROWS=0 . It redraws changed rows instead of scrolling them, for terminals that do not scroll a region of the screen correctly.

title: Troubleshooting
section: Killed at once ( zsh: killed ), or "cannot verify the developer"
text: The executable is quarantined: it was downloaded with a browser. Install with the installer or npm, which do not quarantine, or remove the attribute: xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine rapid-pi-darwin-arm64 .

title: Troubleshooting
section: "Rapid Pi runs on Macs with Apple silicon only"
text: There is no build for Intel Macs. On an Apple silicon Mac, a terminal running under Rosetta still installs the ARM64 build, which runs natively.

title: Troubleshooting
text: In the macOS build, pi is a small launcher, pi-bin next to it is the Rapid Pi executable, and pi-spawn starts the programs Pi runs. Link pi rather than copying it: it starts the pi-bin next to its real path.

title: Troubleshooting
text: codesign may re-sign pi-bin . With the hardened runtime ( -o runtime ), add the entitlement com.apple.security.cs.disable-library-validation ; without it, Rapid Pi runs from bytecode with one notice. The JIT build also needs com.apple.security.cs.allow-jit .

title: Troubleshooting
text: First, check whether the problem is Rapid Pi's: If it also happens with BUN_AOT=0 rapid-pi and with stock Pi, it is Pi's: report it to Pi . If it only happens with Rapid Pi, open an issue with: the output of rapid-pi doctor (the build, installation, extensions and packages, and the problems it finds; no keys or tokens, and your home folder shown as ~ ); on Linux, ldd --version | head -1 ; whether it also happens with BUN_AOT=0 rapid-pi .

title: Troubleshooting
text: When Rapid Pi crashes, it prints "Rapid Pi has crashed", a few lines about the system, and a link that starts with https://rapid-pi.opensec.in/crash/ . The link holds an encoded stack trace and nothing else: no file names, paths or data of yours. Include it in the issue, with what you were doing. The maintainers decode it against that release's symbols.

title: FAQ
text: Help Frequently asked questions Short answers, with links to the details.

title: FAQ
text: Is Rapid Pi a replacement for Pi, or an add-on? It is a complete Pi in one executable: you do not need Pi, Node.js or Bun installed. If you have Pi, Rapid Pi runs next to it as rapid-pi and uses the same configuration, sessions and extensions. Is it a rewrite of Pi? No. Rapid Pi is Pi's own TypeScript source, compiled ahead of time to native code, with a small set of fixes on top. That is why Pi's behavior, commands and extensions carry over. See How it works . Which version of Pi does it run? Run rapid-pi --version . The first number is the Pi release the build is made from: 1.4.0 (Rapid Pi 1.0.0, ...) is Pi 1.4.0. How quickly does Rapid Pi follow new Pi releases? Each new Pi release is merged into Rapid Pi and released after Rapid Pi's tests pass. So far that has taken about a day. Run rapid-pi update to get the latest. Will it change my Pi installation? No. It installs to its own folder and command. Uninstalling it leaves Pi and ~/.pi/agent in place.

title: FAQ
text: Why is the JIT off by default? Pi is already compiled to machine code, so a JIT would only add compiler threads, warm-up and memory. The JIT only helps code loaded at run time, such as heavy extensions. For those, install the JIT build: it keeps nearly all of Rapid Pi's gains, within about 5%. See Choose a build . Why does stock Pi take two minutes to write a 400 KB file? It is not the disk. The file arrives as a streamed tool call in thousands of small chunks, and stock Pi parses and redraws the whole call for each one, so the work grows with the square of the file's size. Rapid Pi processes only the new part. See Benchmarks . Does it make the model faster? No. The model's speed is the provider's. Rapid Pi makes everything around it lighter: launching, drawing long answers, handling large tool calls, and long sessions. That matters most on laptops, with several agents at once, and in scripts. How does it compare with PiG? PiG, a port of Pi to Go, starts sooner, streams with less CPU and peaks lower in memory; Rapid Pi runs Pi's own code, so every Pi extension works unchanged, and it uses less CPU deep into a session and writing files in a terminal. See Against PiG .

title: FAQ
text: Do my extensions work? Yes, unchanged. Extensions that use bun:ffi , such as pi-fff, need the JIT build; opensec-pi-fff gives the same search on the default build. Extensions that start Pi themselves may need to be pointed at rapid-pi . See Extensions . Does it work with Paseo and other tools that run Pi? Yes. Set the tool's Pi command to rapid-pi . See Integrations . Does codemode work? Yes. Codemode is built into Pi and runs in Rapid Pi as it does in Pi: rapid-pi -t +codemode .

title: FAQ
text: Which platforms are supported? Linux on x86-64 or ARM64 with glibc 2.17 or later, macOS 13 or later on Apple silicon, Windows 10 (1809) or later on x64, and Android 7 or later in Termux. See Requirements . Does it run on Linux ARM64, or on Android? Yes, both. Linux ARM64 has its own build, for any 64-bit ARM CPU. On Android, run the installer in Termux: it installs Termux's glibc and sets it as the executable's loader. See Android (Termux) . Is it free? Yes. Rapid Pi is MIT licensed. Release executables include Bun (MIT), JavaScriptCore (LGPL-2.0 and BSD), ICU and Pi (MIT); see THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md .
